Kotlin Multiplatform, from the compiler up · check

Know Kotlin/Native under the hood already?

One question for each of the 6 puzzles in this module. A right answer marks that puzzle as passed, so you can jump ahead. A wrong one tells you which puzzle to start with. Nothing is sent anywhere: it's saved in this browser.

Puzzle 23: From IR to machine code

You change one line in commonMain, then run the app from Xcode with a debug build for the simulator. Which stages run for your shared module?

Right. Compile, then link.

Not quite. Only the link stage writes a binary; the framework isn't updated without it. Learn it in puzzle 23 →

Not quite. The klib holds your module's code as IR, so a changed line means a new klib first. Learn it in puzzle 23 →

Puzzle 24: "One binary: the linker"

Your shared module has a function that no Kotlin code calls, and it isn't in the API Swift can see. After the link stage, is it in the framework?

Not quite. The link stage sees the whole program and leaves out code nothing reaches. Learn it in puzzle 24 →

Right. Unreached and not exported: left out.

Not quite. Only code in the API Swift can see must stay; this function isn't in it. Learn it in puzzle 24 →

Puzzle 25: Static or dynamic

You set your framework's isStatic to true and rebuild the iOS app. On the phone, what does the dynamic loader load for your Kotlin code at launch?

Right. Static: copied in when the app is built.

Not quite. "Static" means joined at build time, not kept in memory. Learn it in puzzle 25 →

Not quite. A static library isn't a separate file on the phone; it's inside the executable. Learn it in puzzle 25 →

Puzzle 26: Framework or XCFramework

You try to merge the iosArm64 framework and the iosSimulatorArm64 framework into one universal framework with lipo. What happens?

Right. Same architecture, two platforms: lipo can't help.

Not quite. lipo can't put both in at all, since they share one architecture. Learn it in puzzle 26 →

Not quite. The halves are told apart by architecture, and these two have the same one. Learn it in puzzle 26 →

Puzzle 27: Reading a crash from the field

You shipped version 3.2 and kept no dSYM. A crash report for 3.2 arrives, so you rebuild 3.2's source today, with the newer Xcode and Kotlin your project uses now, and use that dSYM. What do you get?

Not quite. Same source isn't enough: a build with other tool versions gets another build UUID and may lay out code differently. Learn it in puzzle 27 →

Right. Only the dSYM from that exact build matches.

Not quite. A mismatched dSYM can't be trusted for names either; the addresses may belong to other functions. Learn it in puzzle 27 →

Puzzle 28: Build time and binary size

An iOS developer runs assembleXCFramework after every Kotlin edit, then tries it in the simulator. Which change saves the most time?

Not quite. smallBinary is about size, and it applies to release builds; the time goes into linking every target. Learn it in puzzle 28 →

Right. Build only the binary you run.

Not quite. Then there's no simulator build at all (puzzle 16), and nothing to run. Learn it in puzzle 28 →
